title: Latency numbers and back-of-envelope maths
subtitle: Know the speed of memory, disk and network, and size a system in five minutes with simple maths.

c.v: A food delivery app is about to launch in a new, large city. Arjun owns the order service. His manager asks: "How many servers do we need?"
Arjun does the maths. He expects about 40 million requests a day. He divides by 86,400 seconds and gets about 460 requests per second. A
load test
shows that one server handles about 500. He runs two servers, to be safe.

On the first Friday, at 8 pm, everyone orders dinner at once. Traffic reaches about five times the daily average: over 2,000 requests per second. Both servers hit 100% CPU. Requests wait in queues, and responses take 8 seconds instead of 200 ms.
The app
retries
slow calls, which adds even more load. Orders fail for 40 minutes on the busiest night of the week.
Arjun's maths was correct. His question was wrong. He sized the system for the average second of the day, but users do not arrive evenly. (This story is made up, but the pattern is common.)
Before you build, you should know roughly how big and how fast a system must be. You do not need exact numbers. You need the right
order of magnitude
: is it 10, 1,000 or 100,000 requests per second? Each answer leads to a very different design.
A
back-of-envelope estimate
gets you there in a few minutes. It uses two tools:
The
latency
ladder
How long common operations take, from a CPU
cache
read to a call across the ocean.
Simple traffic maths.
Users → requests per second (
QPS
) → servers, storage and
bandwidth
The key idea.
Round hard and write down your assumptions. Then size for the peak, not the average. A system that is fine on an average day can still crash in its busiest hour.
The latency ladder
These are rough numbers from the well-known table by Jeff Dean and Peter Norvig, as kept up to date by Colin Scott
. They are the values his page shows for recent years. Most are estimates, and your hardware will differ. Learn the
steps between them
, not the exact digits.
To make them feel real, pretend that 1 nanosecond (ns) is 1 second:
Read from the CPU's L1 cache:
about 1 ns (older tables say 0.5 ns) →
1 second
Read from main memory (RAM):
about 100 ns →
under 2 minutes
Random read from an SSD:
about 16 µs (16,000 ns) →
about 4.5 hours
Round trip inside one data centre:
about 0.5 ms (500,000 ns) →
almost 6 days
Round trip from California to the Netherlands:
about 150 ms →
almost 5 years
Three lessons come from this ladder:
Memory is fast, but disk is slow
. So a cache in RAM can save you a lot of time.
A network call costs far more than local work. Avoid calls in a loop.
A call across an ocean costs about 300 calls inside the data centre. A page that makes five such calls, one after another, waits about 750 ms for the network alone.
Numbers to keep in your head
Powers of two are close to powers of ten. 2^10 is about a thousand (KB), 2^20 about a million (MB), 2^30 about a billion (GB) and 2^40 about a trillion (TB)
A day has 86,400 seconds. Round it to
(10^5). Now "per day" to "per second" is just "divide by 100,000". The answer is about 14% too low, which is fine for an estimate.
Network speeds are in
bits
, but file sizes are in
bytes
. One byte is 8 bits, so 100 MB per second needs about 800 Mbit/s.
A worked estimate
Step through Arjun's estimate, done the right way. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys.
The steps are always the same:
Requests per day.
Daily active users
× requests per user. Here: 2 million × 20 = 40 million.
Average QPS.
Divide by 100,000. Here: about 400 QPS.
Peak QPS.
Multiply by a peak factor. Alex Xu's book example uses 2
. Use your own traffic graphs if you have them. A food app at dinner time can be much more uneven. So this example assumes 5, which is a guess, not a measured number.
Servers.
Divide peak QPS by what one server handles in a load test. Then add spare servers, so you survive losing one.
Storage.
Items per day × size × days you keep them. Here: 500,000 orders × 2 KB ≈ 1 GB a day, or about 365 GB a year. One database can hold that.
Bandwidth.
Peak QPS × response size. Here: 2,000 × 20 KB = 40 MB/s, or about 320 Mbit/s.
Peak and average, for latency too
Averages hide problems in latency as well as traffic. Google's SRE book gives an example: a service with an average latency of 100 ms can still have 1% of requests take 5 seconds
. So estimate and measure
percentiles
like p99, not only the average.
Size for the daily average
The busy hour can be many times higher.
Cheapest on paper.
Never for user-facing systems. Fine for batch jobs that can run slower.
Size for the peak, plus spare
You survive the busiest hour and one lost server.
You pay for idle servers at night.
Most new services, and any launch you cannot afford to fail.
Autoscale from the average
Partly. New servers take minutes to start, and sudden spikes arrive faster.
Lower cost when traffic is calm.
Traffic rises slowly and you keep a minimum number of servers running.
Load test with real traffic shapes
You test the real peak, not a guess.
Takes days to build and run well.
Big launches, sales events and systems that move money.
Simple rule:
a quick estimate tells you which design to choose. A load test tells you if the design really works.

sections.name: At work
sections.title: At work: how a senior uses this

c.v: When someone proposes a design, ask:
"How many requests per second at the peak, and how much data per year?"
If nobody knows, do the five-minute estimate together.
Write the assumptions in the
design doc
: users, requests per user, peak factor, sizes
. Others can then correct one number instead of arguing about the result.
Find the peak in real data. Look at the busiest minute of the busiest day, not a daily average. Watch for special days, like a sale, a holiday or a big match.

Remember that the peak can arrive overnight. On 4 January 2021, Slack went from its quietest time of the year to one of its busiest days. Its cloud network hubs (AWS Transit Gateways) did not scale fast enough
Count network calls per request. Each call inside the data centre costs about 0.5 ms. Each call across an ocean, such as California to the Netherlands, costs about 150 ms
Plan for servers to run well below 100% CPU at the peak. Many systems slow down before they reach 100%
. Agree on a target with your team.

"Here are my assumptions: 2 million daily users, 20 requests each, a peak of 5 times the average, 2 KB per order, 20 KB per response. Estimate peak QPS, storage per year and peak bandwidth. Show every step with units."
"List every network call this endpoint makes for one request. Mark which ones run one after another and which run in parallel."
Every number has a unit: per second or per day, bits or bytes, KB or MB.
The estimate uses a peak, not only the average, and the peak factor comes from real data or is clearly labelled as a guess.
The answer is the right order of magnitude. Check one step by hand: divide by 100,000, then multiply by the peak factor.
Latency numbers are treated as rough. AI tools often repeat the old table as if it were exact.
The server count includes spare capacity, so losing one server does not take you down.

Tail latency and queueing
explains why servers slow down sharply as they get busy.

q.v: About how many seconds are in one day, for quick estimates?

why.v: A day has 86,400 seconds. Round it to 100,000 (10^5) to make division easy.

q.v: A service gets 10 million requests a day. The busiest hour runs at 3 times the average. What peak QPS should you plan for?

why.v: 10 million ÷ 100,000 seconds ≈ 100 QPS on average. Three times that is about 300 QPS.

q.v: A read from RAM takes about 100 ns. A round trip from California to the Netherlands takes about 150 ms. How much slower is the round trip?

why.v: 150 ms is 150,000,000 ns. Divided by 100 ns, that is 1.5 million times slower.

q.v: Your estimate says one server is enough for the daily average. What is the biggest risk?

options.v: Traffic is not spread evenly, so the busy hour can be several times the average.
The server will be too fast.

why.v: Users come in waves. Size for the busiest minute, then add spare capacity.
